newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania takes advice of IMF, World Bank on funds.
newsitem.headline: Albania takes advice of IMF, World Bank on funds.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha, responding to advice from the International Monetary Fund and World Bank, has approved legislation to regulate investment schemes to try to prevent further social unrest.

The two world financial bodies urged Berisha to take action quickly to control the schemes after collapses earlier this year caused thousands of Europe's poorest people to lose their life savings and triggered an armed rebellion.
The president's office said Berisha signed a decree late on Monday on the financial control of the investment firms.

"The decree signed by the president answers the suggestions from the International Monetary Fund and World Bank concerning administrators, their functions and competences in the administration of companies carrying out investment activities," the Albanian news agency ATA said, quoting a statement by the president's office.
The legislation establishes rules for creating investment schemes and monitoring their activities and cash flows. It also provides for government-appointed administrators to oversee them.
The IMF in particular wanted international auditors also to look at the schemes, which has now been accepted.
IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus and World Bank President James Wolfensohn urged Berisha in a letter at the weekend to sign the new controls into law.
"Action on this is a precondition for a successful recovery," Camdessus and Wolfensohn said.

Both lenders, it said, were prepared to provide assistance "once Albanian authorities are in control of the country...and have made progress in establishing a sound macroeconomic framework and dealing effectively with the schemes".
The IMF has disbursed about 60 million dollars in credits to Albania since 1992, but loans were suspended in 1995. The World Bank has provided nearly 300 million dollars in credits.
Proposed legislation was initially approved by parliament in May but later amended after the IMF and World Bank expressed reservations about its provisions.
With parliament dissolved ahead of an early general election on Sunday, the law could only be passed by presidential decree.

Zef Preci, the director of Albania's institute for economic research, welcomed the new controls but said the delay in signing the decree meant the law would not take effect until after Sunday's polling.

"Nevertheless, it is a welcome step which, apart from solving the domestic problem, will bring support from the international community to dissolve the companies which are still alive," he told Reuters.

The IMF and World Bank warned the Albanian government last year to crack down on the schemes, which offered huge rates of return to investors with little awareness of markets after 45 years of living in one of Europe's harshest Communist regimes.

Former prime minister Aleksander Meksi said in an interview in the Gazeta Shqiptare daily that events happened so quickly last year that his Democratic Party government was unable to hold back the proliferation of pyramid schemes.

Five "pyramid" schemes, in which interest to old depositors is paid with deposits from new investors, collapsed earlier this year, losing around $1.2 billion of savings, according to government estimates.
Four other schemes remain in operation but have ceased paying the high interest rates initially promised.
Berisha wants the new monitoring procedures to extend to the failed schemes. But the Socialists say those schemes must be dealt with by the courts.
The Socialists are now in government after a coalition administration was formed in March following widespread violence in which at least 1,500 people have died.
